body: There is also the implicit page section without a heading in your example. That is why the rendering differs when you remove section. Furthermore, rendering is only reliable for section and h1, not hn.

As @annevk said, the default stylesheet rules do not map directly to the semantics. This isn't really something we can change, given how web content likely depends on the default rendering and such.

Going to close, but happy to continue discussing in the closed issue, and reopen if we discover there's something we can or should do here.

Thanks for your answers. But I am not sure I understand.

Are you both saying that we agree that the browsers fail to match the specs in the example given, but that’s how it is and we can’t do anything about it? Or do you mean that there is no mismatch between the observed browser’s behavior and the specs?

When writing that “the default stylesheet rules do not map directly to the semantics”, do you mean that the semantics do not cover default stylesheet rules, but that however, the browsers, or other tools, will take other aspects of the semantics of h1 VS h2 into account? Such as screen readers, perhaps?

But, considering that those browsers fail to consider “Foo” as a higher-level heading than “Bar” in their default stylesheet rules in my example above, I suspect, perhaps wrongly, that the browsers or other tools will also fail to distinguish these headings when considering other aspects where the semantics of headings play a role. And that looks to me like a mismatch between the specs and the implementations. If so, I suspect it is possible to align those a bit better.

(Although I fully agree that merely pointing out the existence of a problem is a much simpler matter than proposing a solution, which I’m not even attempting here yet.)

Even if we restrict the discussion to the default stylesheet rules, the semantics of h1 and h2 do, in my opinion, constrain the way a browser should render h1 vs h2 in order to be a reasonable rendering given the semantics. Not that the semantics dictate exactly how those should be rendered, of course, that’s the point of HTML. But rendering h1 and h2 equally is an example of a non-reasonable rendering given the semantics, I’d say.

> When writing that “the default stylesheet rules do not map directly to the semantics”, do you mean that the semantics do not cover default stylesheet rules, but that however, the browsers, or other tools, will take other aspects of the semantics of h1 VS h2 into account? Such as screen readers, perhaps?

More or less. That is, just because something is semantically a level 3 heading, that doesn't mean that the browser's default stylesheet will style it as one.

> I suspect, perhaps wrongly, that the browsers or other tools will also fail to distinguish these headings when considering other aspects where the semantics of headings play a role.

Why would you suspect that? There are two sets of rules defined in the specs: one for rendering, and one for semantics. They are very clearly specified and separate.

There is a separate question of whether and how accessibility tools respect the specced semantics at all, or whether they completely disregard them in favor of just the numeric `<hN>` designator. That has been discussed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/83. Several people assure us that popular accessibility tools ignore them, which brings up the question of whether it's a problem to specify semantic meanings that certain tools disrespect, or whether that's fine because semantics are useful to authors and other tools apart from how they manifest in accessibility technology. I tend to think it's a problem, as I stated in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/83#issuecomment-167440711, but the work hasn't been done yet to address it.

But no tools use the rendering rules as a guide to semantics.

> Even if we restrict the discussion to the default stylesheet rules, the semantics of h1 and h2 do, in my opinion, constrain the way a browser should render h1 vs h2 in order to be a reasonable rendering given the semantics.

I guess I see this point of view, but don't think it's a big deal, given how as you said the whole point of HTML is that semantics and presentation are separate. If the default stylesheet rules are inconvenient for your particular web page structure, overwrite them! Just like the assumption that bold face is a reasonable rendering for `<strong>`, the assumptions baked into the default rendering for headings do not always hold.

> just because something is semantically a level 3 heading, that doesn't mean that the browser's default stylesheet will style it as one.

(…)

> the whole point of HTML is that semantics and presentation are separate. If the default stylesheet rules are inconvenient for your particular web page structure, overwrite them! Just like the assumption that bold face is a reasonable rendering for `<strong>`, the assumptions baked into the default rendering for headings do not always hold.

I believe that the semantics do constrain the set of  possible renderings that may be considered a reasonable implementation of the specs. One of the values of HTML is (IMHO) that an author may rely on the default presentation rules as generally satisfying the semantics written in the specs.

Let me consider an extreme hypothetical case just to make my point clear. Assume all browsers would render `<strong>` by hiding the content, or displaying it in very small letters in a footnote. Then, in my understanding, we could say that there is a mismatch between the specs and the implementation, because such a situation would invalidate parts of [3.2.1 Semantics](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#semantics-2) and [4.5.3 The strong element](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#the-strong-element).

The situation seems to me similar (though much less extreme) with current browsers rendering first-level exactly as second-level headings, in the above example. This behavior could be considered reasonable _if_ we faced a browser that has chosen to always render headings equally, as a stylistic choice. In the current situation however, this is not the case: browsers which usually would render differently different levels of headings cease to render them differently because of the specific encoding of the provided example. This, it seems to me, shows that there is a mismatch between spec and implementation.

I agree this issue is closely related to [#83](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/83), but I think this example shows that the problem with `<section>` and the like go beyond AT.
